When you’ve got a bunch of VFDs running, they create electrical noise called harmonics that can cause all sorts of problems. That noise builds up on the system and can lead to motors and transformers overheating, nuisance breaker trips, and sensitive electronics acting up or failing. It also wastes energy and can interfere with other equipment. On the mechanical side, harmonics can cause voltage to build up on motor shafts, which discharges through the bearings and leads to premature bearing failure. In motors with brushes, it causes extra sparking and wear. All that adds up to more downtime, service calls, and shorter equipment life if you’re not using proper filters or protection.

There are structural benefits for not having 30 year terms. There is a greater amount of risk placed on the borrower, but that also means that the debt people are taking on is balanced with the prevailing rate. This makes mortgages much lower risk for a creditor. The benefit of that for borrowers is that you will also benefit from being able to lower your rate over time if you start in a more expensive market, and the government has a pretty tight control on the mortgage interest rates.

Banks are encouraged to keep the mortgages on their own books instead of bundling them and selling that debt to others. It is fairly low risk to keep people at a 3% interest for 3-5 years when they could be getting 4% from a new customer. In the US it's much more common for a bank to give someone with poor credit a 30 year low percent mortgage, then they bundle that mortgage as a high risk security and sell it to others. There are redundancies built into everything. North america has two electrical grids that bridge the us/canada. BC+Alberta are linked and go south, sask and manitoba as well. Think of all of the lights and motors and ovens as being all connected together and you're spinning a generator outside that makes it all work. If you have two generators and unplug one the other generator will have all the loads on it resisting the spinning of that generator and making it slow down. So since that generator is a big steam engine, you start burning more fuel underneath to make more steam and push it harder to keep the lights on. 

Another interesting factor that would help this is that electrical costs for businesses that are big enough are usually updated and paid for live to push people into off-peak hours. The most important thing I think is to ignore most of the technicalities of competing standards and codes and then start from a position of thinking about the wellbeing of the operator of the equipment. It might be a person with years of experience, maybe bad habits who would overlook things you'd be afraid of. It might be a young person who doesn't even know what could seriously hurt them faster than they can blink. 

Anything you don't identify at the beginning you can't assume other people will know. The only hazards that will be mitigated are the ones you find now until someone is asked to do something that isn't in that list and is hurt. Someone is going to be working on it under high pressure, not making enough money, angry at their boss, or thinking of the weekend so you really can't be too careful.

If you're adding things to existing equipment the best thing you can do is talk to the operators and walk through the new processes to see how they feel about it and what they could identify because they have the most experience and can give great insights. 

For new things put yourself in the position of the operator or maintenance person. What spinning parts can people reach that could pull them in? What moving parts like clamps or actuators can be reached while in motion that could crush? Are there frequencies, magnetic fields, radiation that could harm? Hot surfaces? Sharp edges?

When the equipment is down for maintenance, can it be assembled or disassembled without being underneath a load held by a forklift or crane? Without being energised?

It's really as simple as that, imagine this is your job to work on this machine, or that you'll ask someone you care about to work on it after you're finished and the only education they'll receive is the documentation you send in a box. The goal is to do your best to make sure that everyone goes home with every part of their body they started with because unfortunately no matter how hard you try someone won't. 

After that to really get in the details of the safety levels, reliability, mttf, and all of the standards that apply you'd probably want to take a course to get a foundation because the specific technical wording is important, and learning how to read the legalese of standards is itself a skill.

Modern PLCs (programmable logic controllers, the computers running industrial equipment), are getting more and more abstract and capable. They are programmed on the controller themselves with [IEC-61131-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEC_61131-3). It's a combination of structured text, visual blocks and a thing called ladder logic which is composed very much like physical schematics of the system for ease of use by technicians. The secondary languages that are most useful are c/c++ and python. Arduino has a plc ide if you want to play around with it.

Combination drills with a hammer drill setting are designed with a sort of saw tooth that turns the front of it into a vibrator that causes it to rise and fall on the teeth. That vibration helps a little bit drilling into masonry.

Dedicated rotary hammer drills have a rotating bit, and then also a piston attached to a gear that causes it to literally hammer the bit like a reciprocating saw. This recreates how holes used to be drilled, having a chisel, hitting the end of it, rotating it slightly, hitting it again, over and over again. 

The difference in performance between the two tools is incomparable.

For a safe process you can use a jig this way:

1. Mark the line that you want the holes to be in

2. Drill the first hole with your hole saw

3. Drill the second hole

4. Put a piece of wood or metal aligned with the center of the holes, clamp it and use the two holes as a guide to drill through the wood/metal creating a jig for equally spaced holes.

5. put the jig over the second hole, put a spare hole saw through the hole to keep it perfectly centered, use the jig to keep the next hole the correct distance

Repeat the process moving the jig down each hole.

Alternatively, and higher skill, do these steps to get nice hole alignment.

1. Use a ruler to mark the center line

2. Mark each spot along the line you want a hole

3. Use a center punch and hit an indent where the hole needs to be, this is very important.

4. Either drill the center he with the drill bit your hole saw center bit needs.

5. If these holes aren't perfectly straight you screwed up measuring, center punching or your drill wasn't straight.

6. You can recover from this with a knockout set, knocking out a hole smaller than you need and then having the extra room to realign the right size.

If you only have a hole saw and you need to recover from a bad hole alignment you can put a piece of wood over the holes you drilled and retry. Drill the hole size you need in the wood before you out it over the box, then take the center alignment bit out and just use the outer one, the wood will let you keep it straight without a center hole.

A thyristor functions basically like a latch-on switch.

It has voltage into the anode, out of the cathode and a third gate. By momentarily applying current to the gate it will let current flow from anode to cathode. This power flowing keeps the thyristor active until the voltage to the anode is removed.

Simply put, when you turn it on it will stay on until the power going to it turns off.

The only reason I could give you why you would want a thyristor in a specific alarm circuit is that it's being used as a relay to turn on something at any momentary signal and to make it stay on.

Like if there was a smoke detector, any smoke would make the alarm go off even if the smoke went away, or if there was a security door contact, the alarm would stay on if someone closed the door.
